newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo Corp to set up market-risk office.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo Corp to set up market-risk office.

text.p: Sumitomo Corp plans to set up an office of market risk management for all commodities in April, in response to its massive copper trading losses, Sumitomo president Kenji Miyahara said on Wednesday.

He also said that the firm's internal investigation of the $2.6 billion in losses, which it has blamed on unauthorised deals by former chief copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, would take several more months.
Miyahara told a news conference the probe was taking longer than originally expected and added that there was a limit to how much could be revealed by Sumitomo's internal documents alone.
He said, for example, that Sumitomo learned some facts on Hamanaka's activities for the first time from the British Broadcasting Corporation's Panorama television programme shown last week.

He also said that two Sumitomo board members, Akio Imamura, general manager of the non-ferrous metals division, and Ryo Yamakawa, senior managing director, offered to resign as a result of the copper scandal. Akimoto was Hamanaka's direct supervisor when he first revealed his massive losses last June.
Miyahara did not indicate whether Sumitomo would accept the resignations of the two board members.

The trade house earlier announced that Tomiichi Akiyama, who was Sumitomo's president when the copper losses were discovered, had resigned from the post of chairman due to the scandal and been made an adviser to the company.
Miyahara also said that Sumitomo had no intention of withdrawing from copper trading, although it had cut back its copper trading activity following the scandal.
He reiterated that the company continued to give its full cooperation to investigations of Hamanaka's copper trading by British and U.S. regulatory authorities.
"What I can say is we are fully cooperating with them," he told Reuters after the news conference.

Hamanaka, who until he was fired last June was known in copper market circles as "Mr Five Percent" due to the heavy influence he wielded, pleaded guilty in a Tokyo court last week to charges of fraud and forgery.
